title: Carpentry and Joinery
summary: Learn practical woodwork: timber types and defects, hand and power tools and safety, measuring, marking and cutting, wood joints and fixings, roofs, floors and site carpentry, and finishing and running a carpentry business. Calculations were checked in code.
audience: Apprentices, DIY learners and anyone starting in carpentry, joinery or furniture making

body.p: Carpentry and joinery work with wood to build and make things. Carpenters usually work on site, building roofs, floors, formwork for concrete and door frames; joiners usually work in a workshop, making doors, windows, cabinets, furniture and stairs. Both start with understanding timber.

list: Softwoods come from conifers such as pine and are widely used for roof trusses, framing and formwork. They are usually cheaper and faster growing.

Hardwoods come from broad-leaved trees such as mahogany, teak, iroko, meranti and African hardwoods like mukwa and kiaat. They are often denser and more durable, used for furniture, flooring and doors.
Manufactured boards such as plywood, MDF, chipboard and blockboard are stable, come in large sheets and are used for cabinets and panels.

body.p: Fresh timber contains a lot of water. As it dries, it shrinks and can warp, twist or split, so it should be seasoned (air- or kiln-dried) before use. Look for defects such as large knots, splits, warping and insect or fungal damage. Termites are a major threat in much of Africa; treated timber or naturally resistant species help.

body.tip: Store timber flat, off the ground, under cover and with spacers so air can circulate.

list: Measuring and marking: tape measure, steel rule, try square, combination square, marking gauge and a sharp pencil or marking knife.
Saws: crosscut saws cut across the grain; rip saws cut along it; tenon saws cut joints; coping saws cut curves.
Planes smooth and straighten wood; chisels cut joints and recesses, struck with a mallet.
Hammers, nail punches, screwdrivers, clamps and a spirit level.

body.p: Circular saws, jigsaws, drills, routers, sanders and planers speed up work but cause serious injuries if misused.

list: Wear eye and hearing protection, and a dust mask when sanding or cutting boards such as MDF.
Keep guards in place and blades sharp; blunt tools slip and need more force.
Unplug tools before changing blades or bits.
Clamp the work; never hold small pieces by hand near a blade.
No loose clothing, jewellery or long hair near spinning tools.

body.tip: A sharp chisel is safer than a blunt one; learn to sharpen on an oilstone or waterstone early.

body.p: "Measure twice, cut once" is the first rule. Work from a straight, square reference face and edge, and mark all measurements from them.

A saw blade removes a strip of wood called the kerf, about 3 mm for many saws. Cutting four pieces of 550 mm from a 2400 mm board needs 4 x 550 = 2200 mm plus three cuts of 3 mm = 2209 mm, leaving 191 mm of offcut. Always cut on the waste side of the line.

The 3-4-5 rule: if one side measures 3 units and the adjacent side 4 units, the diagonal will be exactly 5 units when the corner is square, since 3² + 4² = 5². For frames and cupboards, the two diagonals are equal when the shape is square.
Timber is often sold by volume. A piece 50 mm x 100 mm x 3 m has a volume of 0.05 x 0.1 x 3 = 0.015 m³. Twenty pieces make 0.3 m³.

body.tip: Use a marking knife for fine joinery: a knife line is thinner and more accurate than pencil.

body.p: Joints connect pieces of wood. A good joint is strong, accurate and suited to its purpose.

list: Butt joint: two pieces simply meet; weak unless reinforced with screws, dowels or brackets.
Lap and halving joints: each piece is cut to half thickness where they overlap; used in frames.
Mortise and tenon: a tongue (tenon) fits a slot (mortise); a strong, traditional joint for doors, tables and chairs.
Dovetail: interlocking wedge shapes that resist pulling apart; used for drawers and quality boxes.
Dowel and biscuit joints: hidden wooden pins or biscuits align and strengthen joints in boards.
Tongue and groove: used in floorboards and cladding to lock boards together.

body.p: Nails are quick; screws hold better and can be removed; bolts are used for heavy structural work. Wood glue (PVA) makes joints very strong when the parts fit closely. Drill pilot holes for screws to stop wood splitting, especially near the ends of boards.

body.tip: Dry-fit joints without glue first; adjust until they fit, then glue and clamp.

body.p: Site carpentry includes roof structures, floors, ceilings, doors and formwork (temporary moulds for concrete).

For a simple pitched roof spanning 6 m with a rise of 1.5 m, each rafter covers half the span, 3 m horizontally. Its length is √(3² + 1.5²) = about 3.354 m, before adding the overhang. The pitch can be described as rise over run: 1.5 / 3 = 50% (about 26.6°).

list: Roof trusses are often prefabricated and must be braced and fixed as designed; missing bracing is a common cause of roof failure in storms.
Trusses or joists are spaced evenly. For a 3.6 m wall with spacing of 400 mm, you need 3.6 / 0.4 = 9 spaces, so 10 members.
Ceiling boards and sheets are estimated by area: a 4.2 m x 2.4 m wall needs 4 sheets of 1.2 m x 2.4 m.
Door frames must be plumb and square for doors to close properly.

body.tip: Fix roof sheets and trusses with the right number of straps and screws; wind uplift tears off roofs that are under-fixed.

body.p: Finishing protects wood and makes it attractive.

steps: Plane and sand the surface, working from coarse to fine sandpaper, following the grain.
Fill holes and gaps with wood filler.
Apply stain if needed, then the finish: oil, varnish, lacquer or paint.
Sand lightly between coats for a smooth result.

body.p: Outdoor timber needs preservatives and exterior finishes to resist sun, rain and insects. Recoat regularly.

Many carpenters run workshops making furniture and fittings. Accurate quoting (materials, wastage, labour hours, overheads and profit), meeting deadlines, using good-quality timber and keeping customers informed build repeat business. Training routes include apprenticeships, vocational colleges and trade tests.

Safety and care continue after the work is done: store finishes and solvents in sealed containers away from heat, and dispose of oily rags safely, because rags soaked in linseed oil can catch fire on their own.

body.tip: Keep photographs of finished work as a portfolio to show new customers.
